blocks.text: It should be noted in passing that the books of the Arabs mention certain woods so similar to ebony that some take them for ebony. Among these is the wood شيز [shīz] Siz, or شيزي [shīzī] Siza, so called from a place; and the wood ساسم [sāsam] sasem, or سمسم [simsim] semsem, in the plural سماسم [samāsim] semasim, called by the same name as sesame, although it is entirely different from sesame. To this belong these words in Alcamus: الشيز والشيزي خشب اسود للقصاع وهو الابنوس والساسم او خشب الجوز وناحية بارض بادر بيجان [al-shīz wa-l-shīzī khashab aswad li-l-qiṣāʿ wa-huwa al-abanūs wa-l-sāsam aw khashab al-jawz wa-nāḥiya bi-arḍ bādr bījān] Siz, or Siza, a black wood for making dishes. It is either ebony, or sasim, or the wood of the walnut; and also a certain region in the land of Adarbigian (that is, the Atropatia of Strabo and [II, 720] the Atropatena of Ptolemy), from which, namely, this wood is brought and takes its name. The same author elsewhere: الساسم شجر اسود او الابنوس او الشيز او شجر يعمل منه القسي [al-sāsam shajar aswad aw al-abanūs aw al-shīz aw shajar yuʿmal minhu al-qisī] Sasim: a black tree, or ebony, or siz, or a tree from which bows are made. Damir, in the chapter On سمسمة [simsima] simsima, which is a kind of red ant, like שומשמנא among the Chaldeans, says that this same wood is called سمسم [simsim] semsem, in the plural سماسم [samāsim] semasim. He proves this from these words of the pseudo-prophet about الجهنميين [al-jahannamiyyīn], that is, about those who are tormented in Gehenna: تخرجون من النار بعد ان يكونوا فيها فيخرجون كانها عيدان السماسم [takhrujūn min al-nār baʿd an yakūnū fīhā fa-yakhrujūn ka-annahā ʿīdān al-samāsim] They will come out of the fire after some stay in it; they will come out, I say, like the woods semasim, that is, equally black from being scorched by the fire. On these words the commentators offer many quite absurd things. But the more learned recognize that the semasim woods are ebony woods, or woods resembling ebony in blackness, so that they seem burnt. This throws light on these words of Dioscorides in the chapter On ebony: Ἔνιοι δὲ τὰ σησάμινα, ἢ ἀκάνθινα ξύλα ἐμφερῆ ὄντα, ἀντὶ ἐβένου πωλοῦσι· [Enioi de ta sēsamina, ē akanthina xyla empherē onta, anti ebenou pōlousi]. Marcellus Virgilius rendered this as follows: Some sell in place of ebony the timber of the Indian thorn, or of the mulberry, the resemblance deceiving. He thinks, namely, that σησάμινα [sēsamina] should be read συκάμινα [sykamina], because sesame has nothing in common with ebony. But neither has the sycamine or sycomore, except that both are wood. Beware, therefore, of changing anything. For sesamina here means something other than in common usage: namely, the wood of that tree which is called sasim and semsem in Arabic, and in the plural semasim. Accordingly the Arabic translator of Dioscorides rightly has here: ومن الناس من ياخذ اعضان خشب بعض اصناف الشوك والخشب الذي يقال له سيساما فيبيعه بدل الابنوس لانه [col. 145] شبيه به [wa-min al-nās man yaʾkhudh aʿḍān khashab baʿḍ aṣnāf al-shawk wa-l-khashab alladhī yuqāl lahu sīsāmā fa-yabīʿuhu badal al-abanūs li-annahu shabīh bihi] There are some who take the wood of a certain kind of thorn, and the wood which they call sesamum, and sell it in place of ebony, because it resembles it. What is more, besides Dioscorides, Arrian too in the Periplus mentions φαλάγγων σησαμίνων, καὶ ἐβενίνων [phalangōn sēsaminōn, kai ebeninōn], beams of sesamine and of ebony, which are brought from the Indian city of Barygaza to Persia. This reading is therefore certain and beyond doubt.
